faqs.q: What does wildlife removal cost in Flemington?
faqs.a: Pricing turns on the species involved, the height and condition of the roofline, and whether droppings or nesting debris need cleaning out afterward. A Flemington Victorian with a bat colony and a circle-area split-level with one squirrel entry sit far apart in scope, and the written quote, removal, sealing, and cleanup as separate lines, is what makes that plain. Every job starts with an inspection; you get the full figure in writing before removal or sealing begins, and nothing is quoted sight-unseen over the phone.

faqs.q: I can hear baby animals in my Flemington wall — can you just seal the hole?
faqs.a: Not yet, and any company offering to should worry you. Sealing a mother out with a litter inside converts a removal into dead animals in the wall. Spring calls in the borough often start as faint chirping in a chimney wall, and the flue gets a camera check before anyone talks about caps, because a litter changes the whole sequence. We locate the litter first, then time the work so the family leaves or is taken out together — one-way exits sized for the species, or hands-on removal where the young cannot climb. The hole gets sealed the same visit the last animal is confirmed out, not before.

Flemington.wildlife_intro:
Flemington is Hunterdon's county seat, a borough of Victorian and colonial homes along Main Street and the old neighborhoods behind it, ringed by Raritan Township's subdivisions and farms. The borough core carries the old-house catalog: raccoons in the brick chimneys, bats in the tall attics, squirrels at the eaves of a hundred additions. The ring outside adds groundhogs in every garden, skunks under the farm outbuildings, and rats around the older commercial blocks near the circles. It is a small town where the habitat, farmland and creek bottoms, starts a few streets from the courthouse.

Masonry chimneys deserve a slow look. Mortar joints crumble at the crown, flashing lifts where the stack meets the roof, and an uncapped flue reads to a raccoon like a hollow tree. Sealing here is masonry work as much as animal work: a correctly sized cap, repointed joints where they have failed, and flashing reset so water stays out along with the wildlife. Brick and stone stacks on older houses often hide a second, unused flue that nobody remembers — exactly the sort of quiet, warm shaft a denning animal chooses in March. Flemington's chimneys include some of the oldest residential stacks in the county, and the cap and crown work here is planned with the same care as the animal work it finishes.

faqs.q: I found a snake in my Clinton yard — could it be venomous?
faqs.a: Possibly, in this part of New Jersey, which is why identification comes before everything. The northern copperhead (state-Threatened) favors rocky, wooded slopes here, and the timber rattlesnake (state-Endangered) holds on along the ridges; both are left strictly alone and referred to NJ Fish & Wildlife's Venomous Snake Response Team. Clinton's rocky, wooded slopes are copperhead terrain on paper and occasionally in fact, which is why a thick-bodied, banded snake here gets photographed from a distance and identified before anyone reaches for it. Most calls turn out to be harmless black rat snakes or garter snakes, which we can catch and release outdoors within 200 meters, as state policy allows.

faqs.q: Can you get a raccoon family out of a Clinton chimney?
faqs.a: Yes, and spring families are handled as families. A mother raccoon picks an uncapped flue because it mimics a hollow tree, and pups too young to climb are never sealed in or left behind — we check the flue first, reunite or remove the litter with the mother, and fit a proper cap once the chimney is empty. The downtown chimneys are stone and brick from the mill era, and their wide flues have hosted raccoon families for as long as anyone here can remember; a fitted cap ends a very old tradition. Raccoons are a New Jersey rabies-vector species, so the work is done with that caution built in.

Clinton.wildlife_intro:
Clinton is Hunterdon's postcard river town: the Red Mill and the iron bridge on the South Branch of the Raritan, a compact historic downtown of stone and frame homes, and Spruce Run Reservoir just up the road. The river runs through the call log. Raccoons fish the banks and den in the downtown chimneys, bats hold the attics of the older homes along the water, groundhogs dig the riverside lots, and the wooded hillsides around town hold copperhead country a careful distance from the gardens. Squirrels work the big street trees into the eaves all fall.

Look at the trees before blaming the roof. A limb within jumping distance is a bridge, and squirrels treat overhanging branches the way people treat a front walk. Part of lasting proofing is arbor advice: limbs cut back several feet from the roofline, ivy stripped off walls where it gives climbers a ladder, and dense shrubs against the foundation thinned so animals lose their covered approach. Chimney and vent covers handle the rest. Houses under heavy canopy are never one-visit houses — the pressure is constant, so the sealing has to be thorough rather than quick. Clinton's street trees overhang some of the oldest roofs in the county, so the limb report here is part of the animal report, not an afterthought.

faqs.q: Can you get a raccoon family out of a Raritan Township chimney?
faqs.a: Yes — spring raccoon mothers choose uncapped chimneys across Hunterdon County. Our crew checks whether pups are present before anything moves, removes the family together whenever we can, and fits a proper chimney cap so the same chimney is not a den again next spring.

faqs.q: When is wildlife pressure worst in Raritan Township?
faqs.a: Spring denning and the fall push indoors are the two busy waves in Hunterdon County, with bat colonies and mole damage peaking in summer. If you are hearing noise or seeing digging in Raritan Township, calling at the first sign almost always makes for a simpler, cheaper job.

Raritan Township.wildlife_intro:
Raritan Township gives our crew a Hunterdon mix shaped by South Branch of the Raritan River and the Hunterdon plateau and the housing around it. Groundhogs under barns and shed foundations are the everyday Hunterdon call, bats colonize the attics of Flemington, Clinton and Lambertville's older homes every summer, and the Sourland and Cushetunk edges add black rat snakes in barns and the isolated copperhead colonies the county is known for — and Raritan Township is squarely part of that pattern, with raccoons and gray squirrels in attics, skunks and opossums under decks, and seasonal bat work in the older rooflines.

Flemington, Clinton and Lambertville keep Victorian and Federal river-town stock, Readington and Raritan are farmhouses and estate homes on large lots, and High Bridge adds older mill-town housing. In fall and winter, squirrels and rodents push into warm attics and wall voids in Raritan Township; spring brings denning raccoons and groundhog and skunk activity in yards, and summer is bat and mole season. Most Raritan Township jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing of every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

faqs.q: A groundhog is burrowing under my Readington Township foundation — how bad is that?
faqs.a: Worse than it looks. A groundhog burrow system runs many feet with several chambers, and soil removed from under a slab or footing leaves voids that crack concrete and channel water against the foundation. Readington's field soils let a groundhog run a burrow under a whole barn aisle, and the entrances at the fence line and the foundation are usually the same system, which is how the trapping plan treats them. We trap at the active entrances, then backfill and screen the site so the next groundhog inherits a closed burrow. Groundhogs are on New Jersey's rabies-vector list — one more reason not to corner one yourself.

faqs.q: Are wildlife operators licensed in New Jersey?
faqs.a: New Jersey does not issue a wildlife-control-operator license, and any company implying otherwise is dressing up the truth. The legal basis is the Game Code, N.J.A.C. 7:25-5.21: for species like raccoon, squirrel, skunk, opossum, and groundhog, work is done as the property owner's designated agent, and species outside that list are handled under a NJ Fish & Wildlife depredation permit. On a Readington farmstead the designated-agent paperwork covers a property with three structures and four species in a typical visit, which is exactly the situation the Game Code framing was written for. That designated-agent paperwork is part of how a job here is set up.

Readington Township.wildlife_intro:
Readington is one of Hunterdon's big farm townships: the villages of Whitehouse Station and Three Bridges, miles of horse farms and field roads, Cushetunk Mountain rising in the middle, and subdivisions tucked between the farms. The wildlife is farm-country wildlife at full strength. Groundhogs undermine fences, sheds, and foundations in the soft valley soils; raccoons take barn lofts and farmhouse attics; bats hold the older homes in the villages; skunks den under every outbuilding; and Cushetunk's rocky woods are copperhead ground that the surrounding homeowners respect.

On farm and acreage properties the house is only part of the job. Barns shelter raccoon families in haylofts, groundhogs undermine run-in sheds and fence lines, and skunks take up residence under equipment sheds where they are discovered by smell. We plan the property as a whole — which structures to proof, which burrows to treat, where trapping effort actually pays — instead of chasing one animal at a time. Grain and feed storage gets the same attention as the house foundation, because spilled feed is usually what drew the animals to the buildings in the first place. Readington properties are quoted whole, house, barns, and run-ins together, because a township animal problem is a farmstead problem, not a single-structure one.

faqs.q: We keep catching rats around our Lambertville home — why do they come back?
faqs.a: Because the route and the restaurant are still open. Norway rats commute along fence lines, ivy, and utility runs, and they stay where trash, pet food, or a bird feeder feeds them every single night. Lambertville's restaurant blocks feed the alleys behind them, and the rowhouses on those alleys stay rat-quiet only when the building entries are mortared and the alley food is locked down; we plan both halves with the owner. We map the runs, seal the building entries in metal and mortar — rats gnaw through foam and wood — and go over the sanitation changes that make the property stop paying out. Trapping alone, without those two halves, is a subscription, not a solution.

faqs.q: Can bats be evicted from my Lambertville attic in the summer?
faqs.a: Not in midsummer. NJ Fish & Wildlife guidelines limit bat evictions to April 1 through May 14 and August 1 through October 15, because flightless pups would be trapped inside during the May 15 to July 31 maternity stretch. The big homes on the hill hold summer colonies that are usually discovered during a renovation, and mid-season discoveries here get sealed living spaces now and a dated August exclusion, in writing. The work is exclusion only: one-way exits fitted during an open window, left in place through several mild nights, then every gap sealed once the colony has left. Bats are never trapped or killed — they are protected under the state's Endangered and Nongame Species Conservation Act.

Lambertville.wildlife_intro:
Lambertville is a Delaware River town of stone rowhouses, Federal singles, and Victorian cottages packed onto a steep bank between the river and the canal. The housing is old, attached, and full of character and gaps. Raccoons den in the chimneys and porch roofs along the side streets, rats work the riverfront restaurant blocks and the alleys behind them, bats hold attics in the bigger homes on the hill, and groundhogs dig the terraced gardens above the canal. Across the bridge is Pennsylvania; the animals, commuting along the river, do not care.

Attached housing changes the math. In a rowhouse or twin, one animal in a shared attic or party-wall void is every neighbor's problem, and sealing a single unit while the adjoining roofline stays open just moves the tenant sideways. We inspect the whole run of connected rooflines where access allows, coordinate timing with neighbors when entries cross property lines, and seal the full set of openings under one plan. Older masonry party walls hide voids that let squirrels travel between houses unseen — finding those routes is most of the job in attached stock. Lambertville's stone rowhouses share walls and roof voids, so a sealing plan here is drawn for the run of houses, with each entry listed under its owner's name in writing.

faqs.q: Once the animals are out of my High Bridge home, how do I keep them out?
faqs.a: Walk the house the way an animal does: roofline first, then vents, then ground level. Chimney cap, metal-backed vent covers, limbs cut back off the roof, trash in lidded cans, and no pet food or open seed stored in the garage. High Bridge houses sit against gorge woods, so the fall list here runs to the wood line: woodpiles moved off the foundation, brush cut back from the walls, and the terrace-level gaps sealed where the slope meets the house. We leave you the entry map from your own job — which gaps were sealed and which aging spots to watch — because the houses that stay quiet are checked each fall, not just fixed once.

faqs.q: Groundhogs keep raiding my High Bridge garden — what actually works?
faqs.a: Fences alone rarely do; groundhogs climb and dig. What works is removing the animals that have claimed the yard and closing the den they commute from, which is usually under a deck, shed, or brush line rather than in the open. Terraced High Bridge gardens sit directly uphill from burrows in the terrace banks, and the groundhog's commute is a flight of stone steps; the bank, not the garden, is where the work happens. Trapping is set at the burrow mouth, and once the site is clear we backfill and screen it. A garden next to an occupied burrow is a salad bar with a commute of about ten feet.

High Bridge.wildlife_intro:
High Bridge is a small borough in a river gorge: older homes climbing the hillsides above the South Branch of the Raritan, the Columbia Trail heading out along the old rail line, and woods in every direction. The gorge concentrates the wildlife. Raccoons and bats work the hillside houses, groundhogs dig the terraced lots, squirrels come in off the trail-side trees, and the rocky, wooded slopes around the borough are copperhead terrain that locals learn young. A house here can be fifty feet from deep woods and still be on a paved street.

Yard damage tells its own story. Groundhog burrows throw fans of excavated soil against foundations, skunks leave neat cone-shaped holes hunting grubs, and moles push ridges and mounds across lawns that were level in April. Treating the yard means reading which animal made which sign — the remedies differ completely — and fixing the conditions underneath: grub-heavy turf, brush piles, and woodpiles stacked against the house. Burrows at foundations get backfilled and screened once the animals are out; a hole simply filled with dirt is a hole an animal reopens in a night. High Bridge lots are terraces cut into a gorge, and the burrow and den survey here walks every terrace level, because the animal's address is rarely the level the homeowner expects.
